MSK-Skin · Week 14 · Lecture 3 · Lecture Companion

Red, Scaly Rashes: Papulosquamous Diseases

Loretta S. Davis, MD · Medical College of Georgia · Primary source: 43-page professor slide deck

← Week 14 HubCondensed Factoid →PsoriasisClinical variantsTreatmentPityriasis roseaLichen planusSeborrheic dermatitisDifferential
BIG PICTURE. “Papulosquamous” describes well-defined scaly papules or plaques, not one disease. Use morphology (type of scale, color, configuration), distribution, associated nail/mucosal changes, and selective histology to separate psoriasis, pityriasis rosea, lichen planus, seborrheic dermatitis and mimics. The uploaded slides do not provide a formal learning-objective list, so the sections follow the instructor’s teaching sequence rather than inventing objectives.

1 · Recognizing papulosquamous morphology

A papule is a raised, circumscribed lesion; a plaque is a larger raised, relatively flat-topped lesion. Scale reflects excess or abnormal stratum corneum. Professor Davis defines this group by a papule/plaque, scale, and well-defined margins (slide 2). The morphology alone does not name the diagnosis: silvery-white scale, greasy scale, and a collarette of scale imply different disorders.

Clinical reasoning sequence: morphology → distribution → nail or mucosal findings → course/trigger → pathology when needed → targeted treatment.

2 · Psoriasis vulgaris

Mechanism and epidemiology

Psoriasis is a chronic, immune-mediated inflammatory disorder. The lecture emphasizes IL-23 and IL-12 → IL-17-producing T cells and the inflammatory cytokines IL-17, TNF-α and IFN-γ. These cytokine pathways contribute to altered keratinocyte growth and characteristic epidermal thickening/scaling; this mechanistic connection also explains why cytokine-directed biologics can work.

The course states a worldwide prevalence of 2–4%, equal frequency in males and females, and age peaks of 20–30 and 50–60 years. Expression reflects genetic predisposition plus a triggering event.

Clinical phenotype and distribution

Look for well-demarcated erythematous papules or plaques with silvery-white scale. Classic extensor sites include elbows and knees. The lecturer stresses several other locations: low back, gluteal cleft, umbilicus, occipital scalp, genitalia, and nails. In skin of different pigmentation, surrounding erythema may be less conspicuous; shape, scale and distribution remain valuable.

Psoriatic nails and joint disease

Nail findings are not cosmetic trivia: the slide explicitly connects nail disease with increased risk for psoriatic arthritis. Recognize nail pitting, onycholysis (distal separation of plate from nail bed), subungual hyperkeratosis, and oil spots. The lecturer estimates that approximately 20% of patients with psoriasis have psoriatic arthritis.

Diagnosis and histopathology

Diagnosis is usually clinical. If histology is obtained, the specific course findings are hyperkeratosis with parakeratosis, regular epidermal acanthosis, decreased granular layer, Munro microabscesses (neutrophils in stratum corneum), thinning of the epidermis above dermal papillary tips, and dilated superficial papillary vessels. Mechanistic chain: rapid turnover → retained nuclei in stratum corneum (parakeratosis); inflammatory neutrophil recruitment → Munro microabscesses; thin suprapapillary plate above tortuous capillaries → easy pinpoint bleeding.

COMMON CONFUSION: Auspitz sign = pinpoint bleeding after scale removal. Koebner phenomenon = lesions appearing at sites of skin injury. They describe different observations.

3 · Psoriasis variants and red flags

Guttate psoriasis presents as multiple small, erythematous scaly papules, often following streptococcal pharyngitis. Inverse/intertriginous psoriasis occurs in skin creases—groin, under folds, gluteal cleft, etc.—where moist skin can reduce the typical dry scale.

Pustular and erythrodermic psoriasis are labeled life-threatening varieties in the lecture. The professor emphasizes withdrawal of systemic corticosteroids as the most common trigger on this slide. Severe generalized skin inflammation requires urgent clinical assessment.

4 · Psoriasis treatment: mechanism maps to therapy

The slides progress from topical care to phototherapy to systemic treatment, with a prominent warning to avoid oral corticosteroids for psoriasis due to rebound/severe flare concerns.

5 · Pityriasis rosea

Lecture features: most common around ages 10–35, an initial larger herald patch, then multiple smaller lesions with a collarette of scale. Distribution follows skin cleavage lines on the trunk, producing a fir-tree / Christmas-tree configuration. Pruritus can be present or absent. The slides describe a possible viral association with HHV-7 or HHV-6—presented as uncertain, not proven.

Recognition chain: Herald patch first → multiple oval smaller scaly lesions → collarette scale → lesions aligned along skin lines.
COMMON CONFUSION: Pityriasis rosea can initially resemble tinea corporis or secondary syphilis; the lecture’s distinguishing clues are herald patch + collarette scale + fir-tree distribution. These are patterns, not 100% specific tests.

6 · Lichen planus (LP)

LP is a mucocutaneous condition of unknown etiology in the slides. The classic morphology is the 5 Ps: pruritic, purple (violaceous), planar (flat-topped), polygonal papules. The professor also highlights the possibility of pink presentation; visual color alone is insufficient. LP may heal with marked postinflammatory hyperpigmentation. The slides note a higher incidence with hepatitis C and list topical or oral corticosteroids as treatment.

Wickham striae are fine, reticulated/lacy white surface lines, including on oral or genital mucosa; some mucosal LP ulcerates. The lecturer emphasizes Koebnerization in LP as in psoriasis. Histology is an interface dermatitis, with inflammatory obscuration of the dermal–epidermal junction and basal cell vacuolization; pigment incontinence explains why lesions heal darker.

FIRST AID CONNECTION: A symptomatic pruritic violaceous papule + oral Wickham striae + bandlike/interface inflammation supports LP. Histologic basal injury connects directly to the course emphasis on pigment incontinence.

7 · Seborrheic dermatitis

Identify erythematous skin with greasy scale. In infants it is cradle cap; in older patients it favors scalp, eyebrows, nasolabial folds, and sometimes midchest. The slides associate more prominent disease with AIDS and neurologic diseases, and illustrate stress-related flares. The professor highlights the lipophilic yeast Malassezia and treatment with ketoconazole; other shampoos include zinc, selenium sulfide, and tar.

Common confusion: psoriasis tends toward thick silvery-white scale and well-demarcated plaques (including occipital scalp); seborrheic dermatitis has more greasy scale with distribution on scalp/face/folds. Both can involve scalp, so localization alone is insufficient.

8 · Important papulosquamous mimics

The lecturer closes with tinea (dermatophyte fungal infection), secondary syphilis, and cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (mycosis fungoides). Their inclusion is a deliberate warning not to diagnose all red, scaly plaques as psoriasis.

9 · Retrieval checkpoints

What histologic features make psoriasis both scaly and prone to pinpoint bleeding?

Hyper/parakeratosis and regular acanthosis generate scale; suprapapillary thinning and superficial dilated vessels produce the Auspitz sign.

How do you recognize guttate rather than plaque psoriasis?

Many smaller erythematous scaly papules; course association with streptococcal pharyngitis.

What are the four characteristic nail findings discussed?

Pitting, onycholysis, subungual hyperkeratosis, oil spots. Nail findings are associated with increased psoriatic arthritis risk.

What makes pityriasis rosea’s eruption recognizable?

Herald patch, collarette of scale, later smaller lesions aligned in fir-tree distribution.

Why can lichen planus heal with dark marks?

Interface injury / basal-cell vacuolization leads to pigment incontinence and postinflammatory hyperpigmentation.

What is the main clinical distinction between psoriasis and seborrheic dermatitis scale?

Adherent silvery-white scale in classic psoriasis versus greasy scale in seborrheic dermatitis; consider distribution and borders as well.

Which severe psoriasis variants and precipitant were highlighted?

Pustular and erythrodermic psoriasis; the lecturer particularly flags systemic-corticosteroid withdrawal.

Master these before moving on

  1. Psoriasis immune → epidermal mechanism: IL-23/IL-12 and IL-17-related inflammation explains plaques and cytokine-targeted biologics.
  2. Clinical vs histologic psoriasis: silvery extensor plaques with nails versus parakeratosis, Munro microabscesses and regular acanthosis.
  3. Herald patch/scale configuration matters: pityriasis rosea's collarette and fir tree must not be confused with psoriasis.
  4. Interface damage predicts pigment change: lichen planus’ basal injury explains marked residual hyperpigmentation.
  5. Not every scaly plaque is psoriasis: explicitly consider tinea, secondary syphilis and mycosis fungoides.

Source: Davis, “Red, Scaly Rashes: Papulosquamous Diseases,” 43-slide course PDF. Professor figures are embedded directly beside relevant explanations.
